title: Synthesis of Composition-Tunable Syngas from Efficiently Electrochemical Conversion of CO2 over AuCu/CNT Bimetallic Catalyst
abstract: Syngas is significant for the chemical industry for the synthesis of a variety of hydrocarbon fuels and chemicals. Different syngas-based products require syngas with different CO/H2 ratios, which depend mainly on the design of the catalyst. Under this background, we successfully synthesized syngas by electroreduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) with a controllable CO/H2 ratio over a AuCu bimetallic catalyst. In contrast to the monometallic Au and Cu catalysts, the AuCu bimetallic catalyst gives a 95.2% of Faradaic efficiency (FE) at only 290 mV on the selective conversion from CO2 to CO. By tuning the Cu/Au ratio and potential during the electrochemical conversion, the H2/CO in the obtained syngas products can be obtained at the wide range of 0.12 to 5.24. We propose that the controllable H2/CO ratio from CO2 is significant in industrial production and will decrease the cost of catalyst fabrication.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Syngas, a mixture of hydrogen (H2) and carbon monoxide (CO), is usually used as an intermediate for the production of chemicals and fuels. As we know, different chemicals or fuels require different H2/CO ratios in syngas:
1,2 a H2/CO ratio of 1 is used for syntheses of aldehydes,3 with a ratio of 2 for methanol, ethanol, and light olefins,4 and a ratio of 3 for methane.5 At present, the syngas is mainly produced from natural gas6,7 and coal gasification,8,9 which requires high temperature/pressure. Besides, some toxic gases such as H2S are produced during the process.10 The most important thing is that the components of the synthesized syngas (H2/CO ratio) cannot be controlled and with the production of a large number of by-products (e.g., tar, methane, and carbon dioxide).11 Thus, the clean syngas with a controllable ratio of H2 to CO produced by green method is significant for downstream industrial applications. Among the different methods for CO2 conversion such as water−gas shift reaction and CO2 hydrogenation,12 electrochemical reduction of CO2,
13−15 and photochemical reduction of CO2,
16−18 the electrochemical conversion is a particularly promising and attractive strategy because of the measurement under mild conditions.19−22 The electrochemical reduction of CO2 can not only mitigate the global greenhouse effect but also produce syngas from renewable and environmental friendly sources with lower carbon emission than fossil fuels. In recent years, a lot of works have been reported for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO.
23−25 It has been reported that Ag and Au have a high catalytic activity for
selectively converting CO2 to CO. 26−30 Cho et al.31 constructed a silver nanowire/carbon nanosheet composite catalyst that produces syngas with tunable H2/CO ratios from 1.7 to 2.2 via electrochemical reduction of CO2. Kim and Youn32 reported a nanoporous sponge structure of gold and this structure showed a high performance for CO2 reduction with a high faradaic efficiency of 86.8%. However, their high costs and the low Faradaic efficiency hinder the development of catalysts using precious metals.28,33 Meanwhile, a lot of works have been published for the Au-transition bimetallic catalysts to decrease the usage of the precious metal. It was reported that the increase of Cu content favors the hydrocarbon production, and the increase of Au content favors the CO selectivity.34 Many works34−37 investigated Au@Cu core−shell nanoparticles for CO2 electroreduction, and the different Cu shell thicknesses showed a significant effect. However, the increase of selectivity and activity using these catalysts still remain a challenge. Therefore, it is significant but still challenging to design and develop efficient and low-cost catalysts for CO2 electroreduction to obtain syngas with controllable ratios of H2 and CO in one-step by designing the component of catalysts. Now, carbon nanotube (CNT)-based materials attracts
more and more attention in the field of electrochemistry due

to their excellent properties such as high surface area and electrical conductivity, chemical stability, and inferior activity of hydrogen evolution reaction.38 In recent years, the reactivity of CNT-supported catalysts for CO2 electroreduction have been widely studied both experimentally and theoretically.39−42 CNTs were very good support for catalysts because metal active particles can be deposited on CNTs using a variety of deposition methods and high dispersion of metals on the CNTs as well as the catalytic properties can be obtained.39 Liu et al.43 reported a N-enriched CNT for the electroreduction of CO2 to CO using pyridinic-N as the active site. However, this metal-free catalytic electroreduction of CO2 did not show very high activity for CO2 conversion compared with Au- or Cu-based catalysts and the H2/CO ratio obtained was in a low range (1:3−3:1). Herein, we reported the production of CO and H2 from CO2 electroreduction by well-defined AuCu bimetallic catalysts using CNTs as support, which were synthesized via aqueous reduction method (Scheme 1). The AuCu bimetallic
structure was characterized by X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and microscopy. A high Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 95.2% and superior catalytic stability were obtained. At last, by changing the ratio of Cu/Au and applied potential (AP), we were able to finely control the H2/CO ratio from 0.12 to 5.24 in the produced syngas, which would be beneficial for practical applications.

sections.heading: 2. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
2.1. Characterizations. The structural properties of CNT, Au/CNT, Cu/CNT, and bimetallic AuCu/CNT catalysts were investigated by XRD measurement (Figure 1a). All catalysts displayed a diffraction peak located at approximately 26.1°, which was attributed to the multiwalled CNT carrier.41 In addition to this diffraction peak, Cu/CNT and CNT exhibited
another two similar diffraction peaks between 40° to 45°, corresponding to other crystalline planes of the CNT carrier.42 It is worth noting that no diffraction peaks corresponding to Cu could be found in Cu/CNT, indicating Cu nanoparticles might exist in an amorphous form or be highly dispersed. For Au/CNT catalysts, the diffraction peaks at 38.2°, 44.4°, 64.6°, and 77.5° were ascribed to the (111), (200), (220), and (311) crystalline plane of Au, respectively, revealing the formation of Au particles. With the addition of Cu, the intensity of diffraction peaks ascribed to Au in bimetallic AuCu/CNT catalysts decreased gradually. Compared to Au/CNT, the main peak around 38.5° shifted to the higher 2θ for the AuCu2/ CNT and AuCu8/CNT catalysts (Figure 1b), revealing that Cu might be incorporated into the Au lattice to form Au−Cu alloy. The BET surface area of CNT is 86.60 m2/g and the BET surface area of AuCu2/CNT is 78.36 m
2/g. To further confirm the formation of Au−Cu alloy, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)-mapping, and line-scanning experiments were performed (Figure 2). TEM image of Cu/CNT in Figure 2a displays the existence of well-dispersed Cu particles, which is also revealed by EDS results in Figure S1. The low crystallinity and highly-dispersed Cu particles might be responsible for the absence of Cu diffraction peaks in XRD results. For the AuCu2/CNT catalyst in Figure 2b, the observed particles were well-dispersed on the wall of CNT with an average particle diameter of 11.5 nm. EDS-mapping result of AuCu2/CNT in Figure 2c reveals that Au and Cu Xray signals are distributed together in the observed metal particles.44 In comparison, the C X-ray signal was detected on the whole sample, indicating that Au−Cu alloys were dispersed on the surface of CNT. Moreover, the line-scanning results of four metal particles further validate the formation of the Au− Cu alloy, in agreement with the shift of Au diffraction peaks in AuCu2/CNT. AuCu2/CNT sample was then characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to investigate the surface chemical states of Au and Cu respectively. The main elements revealed by Figure 3a were Au, Cu, C, and O; and the relative atomic percentage of C, Au, and Cu in the AuCu2/CNT sample was estimated to be 89.7, 0.34, and 2.6%, respectively. As shown in Figure 3b, the spin−orbital splitting peaks at 83.9 eV and 87.6 eV indicated the reduction of HAuCl4 to Au 0 species. The Cu 2p XPS spectrum in Figure 3c exhibited peaks at around 952.9 and 933.3 eV, which could be assigned to binding energy of Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2
, respectively. Moreover, no satellite peaks assigned to Cu2+ could be observed, indicating Cu2+ has been reduced to Cu+ and/or Cu0 species. To further distinguish the Cu species between Cu0 and Cu+, Cu LMM Auger electron spectroscopy was performed in Figure 3d. The low kinetic energy at around 916.5 eV in Figure 3d indicated the surface of AuCu2/CNT was dominated by Cu+, together with a small amount of Cu0.45 The mixture of Cu+ and Cu0 on the surface of the AuCu2/CNT sample might be attributed to the partial reduction of Cu2+or oxidation of Cu0 in air. Figure S3 shows the Raman spectra of Au/CNT, Cu/CNT, AuCu2/CNT, and AuCu8/CNT samples. All spectra suggest two obvious bands at around 1350 cm−1 and 1580 cm−1, which correspond to the D and G bands of carbon materials.41 As reported, the D band indicates the presence of disordered graphite carbon, and the G band suggests crystalline graphite carbon.41 The calculated ID/IG value of four catalysts is similar,

The Cu and Au mass loading in Cu/CNT and Au/CNT were 4.8 and 4.9 wt %, respectively. For AuCu2/CNT catalyst, the Au and Cu mass loadings were 3.1 and 1.9%, respectively. In comparison, the Au and Cu mass loadings were 1.3 and 3.7%, respectively, for the AuCu8/CNT catalyst. The actual molar ratio of Cu/Au in AuCu2/CNT and AuCu8/CNT was 1.9 and 8.0, similar to the theoretical ratio. 2.2. Electrochemical Conversion of CO2. The electrochemical activities of the synthesized AuCu2/CNT bimetallic catalyst were evaluated in Ar- and CO2-saturated KHCO3 solutions. Firstl, the 1 mA/cm2 of current densities recorded at −0.5 V vs RHE under Ar-satuated circumstance is shown in Figure 4a, which showed −0.5 V vs RHE due to the hydrogen evolution reaction. It is much higher than that obtained under CO2-saturated electrolyte (−0.155 V) over AuCu2/CNT. This might be associated with the occurrence of the CO2RR.
43 As shown in Figure S4, AuCu2/CNT exhibits the highest current density and the most positive onset potential, meaning the highest catalytic activity among the Au/CNT, Cu/CNT, and AuCu/CNT with different ratios.46 The results of the catalytic activity of the reduction of CO2 (Figure 4b) also proved the advantage of the bimetallic alloy catalyst. The AuCu2/CNT showed a much larger Faradaic efficiency for CO than that of AuCu8/CNT, Au/CNT, and Cu/CNT, indicating its superior catalytic activity for CO2 electroreduction. The maximum FE displayed by AuCu2/CNT for CO was 95.2%, which occurred at only 290 mV of the overpotential. As a comparison, the
maximum FE values obtained by AuCu8/CNT, Au/CNT, and Cu/CNT were 82.5%, 73.0%, and 35.7%, respectively. Many other catalysts reported so far are summarized in Table S1, which further highlight the better performance of AuCu2/CNT in this work. As characterized by XRD and TEM-mapping (Figures 1 and 2), the superior catalytic activity of the AuCu bimetallic catalyst was due to the synergistic effect of Au and Cu. Then, the Tafel plots are shown in Figure 4c to study the kinetics for CO formation over AuCu/CNT. The Tafel slope at low overpotential for the AuCu2/CNT catalyst was 50 mV/ dec and increased to 97 mV/dec at high overpotential, indicating that the rate of CO formation was greater over the AuCu2/CNT than that of AuCu8/CNT, Au/CNT, and Cu/ CNT.47,48
The controllable composition in syngas still remains an intense interest for the production of different renewable fuels from Fischer−Tropsch (FT) process and hydroformylation.43 Then, as a blank experiment, we tested CO2 reduction over acid pretreatment CNT without Au and Cu under the same conditions, the result shows that no CO is detected and is similar to the results of the AuCu/CNT catalysts electrolysis in an Ar-saturated electrolyte. This confirmed that it is the Au and Cu nanoparticles enhanced the catalytic activity of the CO2 electroreduction. Notably, the ratio of H2 to CO in the produced syngas from Au/CNT in this work can be controlled from 0.12 to 5.24 as shown in Figure 5a by changing the AP. The selectivity of the CO2 reduction electrocatalysts were studied by gas chromatography and 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Only gas products were detected at the cathode side, and the major products are H2 and CO along

with a little CH4 and C2H4, which means that the components of products are similar to the syngas. As reported, Cu is mainly the response to the reaction of CO2RR to produce hydrocarbons such as CH4 and C2H4, while Au to the reaction of CO2RR to produce CO. Thus, it also tuned the H2/CO ratio by tuning the Cu/Au ratio at the same potential, thus making the produced syngas have a very wide range of applications as shown in the Figure 5b−d. As the Cu/Au ratio increased from 1.3 to 31.4, the H2/CO ratio produced by both potentials showed an increased trend and this is corresponding to the decrease of the Cu/Au ratio because Au was reported to mainly respond to the reaction of CO2 electrochemical reduction to produce CO. As shown in Figure S5, the partial current density (PCD) of
CO detected for the series samples increase as the AP. In
contrast, the FE for CO of AuCu2/CNT increases as the potential increases to −0.4 V and gradually decreases as the potential increases further to −1.0 V, which may be due to the competition between the HER and CO2 reduction. AuCu2/ CNT shows a much larger PCD for CO than Au/CNT and Cu/CNT. The electrochemical surface areas (ESA) were evaluated by
the double-layer capacitance (Cdl) values as shown in Figure S7. The values of Cdl over AuCu2/CNT and AuCu8/CNT were 10.94 mF/cm2 and 10.41 mF/cm2, respectively, while the values of Cdl over Au/CNT and Cu/CNT were 9.34 mF/cm 2 and 10.17 mF/cm2, respectively. This result shows that AuCu/ CNT has a large active ESA, which accounts for its superior catalytic activity.

Lastly, the electrochemical catalytic stability was tested at −0.4 V for 20 h and the results are shown in Figure 6. Before
electrolysis, the electrolyte was saturated with CO2 for 30 min, then the CO2 bubbler was switched off, and the cell was kept airtight. With the aid of an electrochemically stable reduction, the electrode was held at −0.4 V vs RHE for 20 h to obtain the amperometric i−t curves. It clearly showed that the AuCu2/ CNT gave almost no reduction of the current density under the condition, and the FE for CO was maintained as high as 90%, indicating the excellent stability of the catalyst. The high stability and other attributes of AuCu2/CNT make it a promising catalyst for the electrocatalytic CO2 conversion to produce syngas.

sections.heading: 3. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In conclusion, we reported an AuCu/CNT electrocatalyst that was facilely synthesized by growing Au and Cu nanoparticles onto multiwalled CNT via an aqueous reduction method. This integrated electrocatalyst displayed very high catalytic activity and stability for the synthesis of clean syngas from CO2 with a controllable H2/CO ratio. An FE as high as 95.2% for CO was obtained in this work. Most importantly, the H2/CO ratio in the syngas product can be controlled in a large range from 0.12 to 5.24. Lastly, the catalyst showed good stability, without any catalytic reduction within 20 h.
